verdicts.flaw_description: The measurement date precedes the intervention date in three of the four cases: 'a lathe at Bexley on nights, fitted 4 May, measured by 27 March', 'a conveyor at Corbin on evenings, fitted 2 August, measured by 21 July', and 'a compressor at Marlowe on weekends, fitted 25 November, measured by 6 October'. Only case two (fitted 9 January, measured by 24 February) has a coherent order, matching the short post-fitting window the template intends. An outcome window that closes before the new bearing was fitted cannot record any effect of it, so three quarters of the evidence is chronologically incapable of supporting the claim.

Outcome measurement is restricted to the fully-exposed subgroup: 'Rates cover the patients whose whole stay ran under the protocol, and a quarter of each ward's patients had spells outside the protocol.' A quarter of patients are dropped precisely because their exposure was incomplete, and time spent off the protocol plausibly tracks longer, sicker, more complex stays - exactly the patients most likely to acquire infections. The reported 6-11 percent reductions are therefore per-protocol figures on a filtered population, not the ward infection rate the claim is about. (The four records are also the same ward in the same quarter with the same auditor, so they are not four independent observations.)

The retention measurement predates the email send in three of the four cohorts: 'starter signups from Norway via webinar were emailed 24 March, measured by 9 March', 'enterprise signups from Vietnam via reseller were emailed 25 October, measured by 10 October', and 'basic signups from Ireland via podcast were emailed 26 December, measured by 2 December'. Only the Chile cohort (emailed 3 July, measured by 27 July) runs in the right order. A week-two retention figure closed out before the onboarding email was sent cannot have been produced by that email.

The timing set is filtered on compliance with the intervention: 'Only runs completed end to end on the issued route entered the timing set, and drivers at each depot abandoned the issued route on roughly one run in six.' Runs are excluded exactly when the new route was abandoned, and drivers most plausibly abandon it on the runs where it was going badly (traffic, blockages, bad sequencing). Dropping roughly one run in six on an exposure criterion correlated with the outcome biases the 5-9 minute improvements downward in duration, so the surviving runs do not establish that the routing change cuts delivery time overall.

An uncontrolled confound moves with the outcome and the report confirms the cohorts were exposed to it rather than shielded: 'Outdoor temperature in each cohort's city ran about four degrees below the month before, and every cohort slept in rooms with no climate control.' Cooler sleeping environments lower resting heart rate on their own, and with no climate control the rooms track the outdoor drop, so the 3-6 bpm declines against a one-month-earlier baseline are equally explained by the seasonal temperature fall as by the app. Note the contrast with the other reports, where the parallel sentence either holds the rival factor constant or insulates the units from it; here it does neither.
